title: Amp Code: Next Generation AI Coding – Beyang Liu, Amp Code

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is Amp Code, a coding agent for software engineering with terminal and editor integration, sub-agent architecture, and a review interface for agentic code output.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is Amp Code, a coding agent for software engineering with terminal and editor integration, sub-agent architecture, and a review interface for agentic code output.

summary: Beyang Liu presents Amp Code as an opinionated frontier agent for AI-powered software development. The company embraces a weird, forward-looking ethos, aiming to live one year in the future where agents write much of the code. Amp runs from the terminal with a custom-built TUI framework that streams diffs and CLI commands while connecting to editors like Emacs, Neovim, and JetBrains for diagnostics. It also installs into VS Code derivatives including Cursor and Windsurf. A key bottleneck identified is code review: users spend most of their time reviewing agent output, which constrains parallelization. Amp addresses this with a dedicated review interface featuring a custom diff viewer, editable diffs, full code navigation, and a guided tour of changes. The core architectural philosophy treats an agent as a for loop with tool calls and a model, giving builders levers over model choice, tool descriptions, and iteration. Amp contrarianly deprioritizes MCP in favor of custom tools, arguing that MCP servers cannot tune tool descriptions to agent goals and that too many tools cause context confusion. Context exhaustion from tool calls is solved via specialized sub-agents: the finder for codebase search, the oracle for deep reasoning, the librarian for external library context, and the experimental Kraken for large-scale refactors. Unlike most coding agents that use a model selector, Amp offers two top-level agents: a slower smart agent with full sub-agent access and a rush agent for quick in-the-loop edits. The smart agent recently switched to Gemini 3, with extensive pre-release testing to optimize for its capabilities. On the UI layer, Amp treats the editor increasingly as a reader for reviewing agentic output while driving edits through an agent panel. The terminal UI leverages modern rendering capabilities with graceful degradation for basic terminals. To help developers learn the new craft of agentic coding, Amp supports thread sharing among teammates. To address cost barriers to adoption, especially for students, Amp shipped a mini ad network delivering subtle ads for developer tools, subsidizing inference costs for the rush agent. Amp positions itself as an agentic research lab targeting builders who want to live in the future, supported by a community run by Ryan Carson.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & The Weird Ethos
sections.summary: Beyang Liu introduces himself and Amp as an opinionated frontier agent. He describes the team as weirdos embracing the awe and absurdity of agents writing code, aiming to be a research lab living one year in the future.

sections.title: Amp Terminal UI & Editor Integration
sections.summary: Amp runs from the terminal with a custom-built UI framework that streams diffs and CLI commands. It connects to editors like Emacs, Neovim, and JetBrains for diagnostics. It also installs into VS Code derivatives, enabling agent-driven code editing through a panel.

sections.title: The Review Bottleneck & Review Interface
sections.summary: Liu identifies code review as the main bottleneck limiting agent parallelization. Most of his time is spent reviewing agent output. Amp built a review interface to streamline understanding what the agent wrote and prevent shipping sloppy code.

sections.title: Defining an Agent: For Loops & Tool Calls
sections.summary: An agent is fundamentally a for loop with tool calls and a model. Builders have three levers: model choice, tool descriptions, and iteration with tools. Despite seeming limited, these produce wide behavioral variance.

sections.title: The Argument Against MCP (Context Confusion)
sections.summary: Amp deprioritizes MCP in favor of custom tools for two reasons: MCP servers cannot tune tool descriptions to agent goals, and too many tools cause context confusion. Custom tools help identify and close feedback loops.

sections.title: Tool Call Context Exhaustion & Sub-Agents
sections.summary: Tool calls consume context, causing premature stops or doom loops. Sub-agents solve this by factoring subtask context into separate windows. Amp has specialized sub-agents: finder for search, oracle for reasoning, librarian for external context, and Kraken for refactors. Unlike competitors using model selectors, Amp offers two top-level agents: smart for complex tasks and rush for quick in-the-loop edits.

sections.title: Model Choice, UI Layer & Learning the Craft
sections.summary: Amp recently switched the smart agent to Gemini 3 with extensive pre-release optimization. The editor is now primarily a reader for reviewing agentic output, with a custom diff viewer, editable diffs, code navigation, and a guided tour of changes. The terminal UI leverages modern rendering with graceful degradation. Thread sharing enables team learning of agentic coding techniques. To address cost barriers, especially for students, Amp shipped a subtle terminal ad network subsidizing rush agent inference. Amp positions itself as an agentic research lab targeting future-leaning builders, with a community run by Ryan Carson featuring interviews and in-person events.
